title: Agentic RAG
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Agentic RAG ##### The query that needed three retrievals A legal-tech team in Pune had a RAG system at 84% accuracy. The remaining 16% were dominated by one query shape: > *"Does the indemnity cap in our Reliance MSA exceed the standard we use for enterprise clients?"* Static RAG embedded that sentence, retrieved five chunks, and produced a confident wrong answer. The chunks were about indemnity generally — none contained the Reliance cap, none contained the enterprise standard, and nothing compared them. The query needs three separate retrievals: find the Reliance MSA indemnity clause, find the enterprise-standard template, then compare. **A fixed pipeline retrieves once and cannot know it needs to retrieve again.** They rebuilt retrieval as an agent loop — retrieve, grade the results, decide whether they suffice, re-query if not. Accuracy went to 93%. Median latency went from 1.9s to 4.4s, and cost per query roughly tripled. **Agentic RAG trades latency and cost for the ability to recognise and recover from its own failures.** Day 19 showed the failure taxonomy; today is the architecture that fixes several categories at runtime rather than at design time. ##### Static versus agentic ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph S["Static RAG"] S1["Query"] --> S2["Retrieve k=5"] S2 --> S3["Generate"] S3 --> S4["Answer"] end subgraph A["Agentic RAG"] A1["Query"] --> A2{"Retrieval
needed?"} A2 -->|No| A9["Answer directly"] A2 -->|Yes| A3["Retrieve"] A3 --> A4["Grade documents"] A4 --> A5{"Sufficient?"} A5 -->|No, wrong terms| A6["Rewrite query"] A6 --> A3 A5 -->|No, missing info| A7["Web search / other source"] A7 --> A8["Generate"] A5 -->|Yes| A8 A8 --> A10{"Answer grounded
& complete?"} A10 -->|No| A6 A10 -->|Yes| A11["Answer"] end ``` The difference is **decisions at runtime**. Static RAG's behaviour is fixed at design time; agentic RAG chooses its path per query based on what it observes. | | Static RAG | Agentic RAG | |---|---|---| | Retrievals | Exactly 1 | 0 to N | | Recognises failure | No | Yes | | Multi-hop | Fails | Handles | | Latency | 1–2s | 3–10s | | Cost | 1× | 2–5× | | Determinism | High | Lower | | Debuggability | Easy | Needs tracing | ##### Retrieval as a tool The conceptual shift from Day 37's agents: instead of a pipeline stage, retrieval becomes a **tool the model chooses to call**. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal RETRIEVAL_TOOLS = [ { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "search_contracts", "description": ( "Search the contract repository for clauses and terms. Use for any " "question about specific agreements, clauses, obligations, or terms. " "Returns excerpts with document name and clause number. " "Call multiple times with different queries when comparing documents." ), "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": {"type": "string", "description": "Natural language search query"}, "document_filter": { "type": "string", "description": "Optional: restrict to a client or document " "name, e.g. 'Reliance MSA'", }, "clause_type": { "type": "string", "enum": ["indemnity", "termination", "payment", "liability", "confidentiality", "any"], }, }, "required": ["query"], }, "strict": False, }, }, { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "search_templates", "description": ( "Search standard contract templates and internal policy standards. " "Use when the question references 'our standard', 'the template', or " "compares a specific contract against policy." ), "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": {"type": "string"}, "tier": {"type": "string", "enum": ["enterprise", "mid_market", "smb", "any"]}, }, "required": ["query"], }, }, }, ] ``` **The description is where the intelligence lives.** "Call multiple times with different queries when comparing documents" is what makes the agent decompose the Reliance question. Without that sentence it retrieves once and stops. **Distinct tools per source** beats one tool with a source parameter. The model routes more reliably when the choice is between named tools than when it is filling in an enum. ##### Document grading The mechanism that lets the agent recognise inadequate retrieval. ```python from openai import OpenAI from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor client = OpenAI() class DocumentGrade(BaseModel): relevance: Literal["relevant", "partially_relevant", "irrelevant"] contains_answer: bool reason: str = Field(..., max_length=200) GRADE_SYSTEM = """Grade a retrieved document against the user's question. relevance: - relevant: directly addresses the question - partially_relevant: same topic, does not answer it - irrelevant: different topic contains_answer: true only if the document alone is sufficient to answer. Be strict. A document about indemnity generally is partially_relevant to a question about a specific indemnity cap, not relevant.""" def grade_document(question: str, doc: dict, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> DocumentGrade: completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=DocumentGrade, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": GRADE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n\nDocument:\n{doc['text'][:1500]}"}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed def grade_documents(question, docs, max_workers=8): """Grade in parallel — sequential grading dominates latency.""" with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool: grades = list(pool.map(lambda d: grade_document(question, d), docs)) relevant = [d for d, g in zip(docs, grades) if g.relevance == "relevant"] partial = [d for d, g in zip(docs, grades) if g.relevance == "partially_relevant"] has_answer = any(g.contains_answer for g in grades) return { "relevant": relevant, "partial": partial, "any_contains_answer": has_answer, "n_relevant": len(relevant), "grades": grades, } ``` **Parallel grading is not optional.** Grading five documents sequentially adds 2–3 seconds; in parallel it adds 400ms. This single detail decides whether agentic RAG is usable in an interactive product. **Use a small model.** Grading relevance is far easier than answering, and `gpt-4o-mini` matches larger models on this task at a fraction of the cost. A fine-tuned cross-encoder is cheaper still. ##### A LangGraph agent LangGraph models the agent as a state machine, which is what makes the loops and conditionals explicit and debuggable. ```python from typing import TypedDict, Annotated, Literal from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END import operator class RAGState(TypedDict): question: str original_question: str documents: Annotated[list, operator.add] generation: str retrieval_count: int rewrite_count: int used_web: bool trace: Annotated[list, operator.add] MAX_RETRIEVALS = 3 MAX_REWRITES = 2 def retrieve_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: docs = vector_retriever(state["question"], k=6) return { "documents": docs, "retrieval_count": state.get("retrieval_count", 0) + 1, "trace": [{"node": "retrieve", "query": state["question"], "n_docs": len(docs)}], } def grade_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: result = grade_documents(state["original_question"], state["documents"]) return { "documents": [], # replaced below via a custom reducer "trace": [{"node": "grade", "n_relevant": result["n_relevant"], "has_answer": result["any_contains_answer"]}], **{"_graded": result}, } def decide_after_grading(state: RAGState) -> Literal["generate", "rewrite", "web", "give_up"]: graded = state.get("_graded", {}) if graded.get("n_relevant", 0) >= 1: return "generate" if state.get("rewrite_count", 0) < MAX_REWRITES: return "rewrite" if not state.get("used_web") and web_search_enabled: return "web" return "give_up" def rewrite_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: prompt = ( f"The search for this question returned nothing relevant.\n\n" f"Original question: {state['original_question']}\n" f"Query tried: {state['question']}\n\n" f"Write a different search query using alternative terminology. " f"Preserve all specific names, codes, and clause numbers exactly. " f"Output only the query." ) new_query = _call_llm(prompt, temperature=0.3).strip() return { "question": new_query, "rewrite_count": state.get("rewrite_count", 0) + 1, "trace": [{"node": "rewrite", "new_query": new_query}], } def web_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: docs = web_search(state["original_question"], k=4) return {"documents": docs, "used_web": True, "trace": [{"node": "web_search", "n_docs": len(docs)}]} def generate_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: docs = state.get("_graded", {}).get("relevant") or state["documents"] answer = rag_generate(state["original_question"], docs[:5]) return {"generation": answer["answer"], "trace": [{"node": "generate", "n_context": len(docs[:5])}]} def give_up_node(state: RAGState) -> dict: return { "generation": ("I could not find information to answer this in the " "available documents. Please rephrase or contact the " "legal team directly."), "trace": [{"node": "give_up"}], } graph = StateGraph(RAGState) graph.add_node("retrieve", retrieve_node) graph.add_node("grade", grade_node) graph.add_node("rewrite", rewrite_node) graph.add_node("web", web_node) graph.add_node("generate", generate_node) graph.add_node("give_up", give_up_node) graph.add_edge(START, "retrieve") graph.add_edge("retrieve", "grade") graph.add_conditional_edges("grade", decide_after_grading, { "generate": "generate", "rewrite": "rewrite", "web": "web", "give_up": "give_up", }) graph.add_edge("rewrite", "retrieve") # ← the cycle graph.add_edge("web", "generate") graph.add_edge("generate", END) graph.add_edge("give_up", END) app = graph.compile() ``` **The `rewrite → retrieve` edge is the cycle**, and it is what static pipelines lack. `MAX_REWRITES` is what stops it looping forever — a hard bound on every cycle is mandatory in agentic systems. **`operator.add` on the `documents` and `trace` fields** makes them accumulate across nodes rather than being overwritten. That accumulation is how the agent builds up evidence across multiple retrievals. ##### Self-correction on the answer Grading documents catches retrieval failure. Grading the *answer* catches generation failure. ```python class AnswerGrade(BaseModel): grounded: bool = Field(..., description="Every claim supported by the context") addresses_question: bool complete: bool = Field(..., description="Covers what the context supports") missing: str = Field("", description="What is missing, if incomplete") ANSWER_GRADE_SYSTEM = """Grade an answer against the retrieved context and question. grounded: false if ANY claim is not supported by the context, including specific numbers, dates, or clause references not present in it. addresses_question: does it answer what was asked? complete: does it cover everything the context supports? Be strict about grounded. A fabricated clause number makes it false.""" def grade_answer(question, context, answer, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> AnswerGrade: ctx = "\n\n".join(c["text"][:1200] for c in context) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=AnswerGrade, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": ANSWER_GRADE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n\nContext:\n{ctx}\n\nAnswer:\n{answer}"}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed def decide_after_generation(state) -> Literal["end", "retrieve_more", "regenerate"]: grade = state.get("_answer_grade") if grade is None: return "end" if not grade.grounded: return "regenerate" # same context, stricter prompt if not grade.complete and state["retrieval_count"] < MAX_RETRIEVALS: return "retrieve_more" # need more evidence return "end" ``` **Distinguish the two failure modes.** Ungrounded means regenerate with the same context and a stricter prompt. Incomplete means retrieve more. Conflating them wastes a retrieval on a prompt problem. **This is Self-RAG's core idea without the fine-tuning** — Asai et al. trained reflection tokens into the model; a separate grader gets most of the benefit with an off-the-shelf model. ##### Iterative multi-step retrieval The Reliance question needs sequenced retrieval where the second query depends on the first result. ```python class RetrievalPlan(BaseModel): reasoning: str is_complete: bool = Field(..., description="Do we have enough to answer?") next_query: str = Field("", description="Empty if complete") next_source: Literal["contracts", "templates", "web", "none"] = "none" ITERATIVE_SYSTEM = """You are gathering evidence to answer a question. Review what you have retrieved so far. Decide whether it is sufficient. If not, specify ONE next search query and which source to use. Rules: - Build on what you already know. If you found the Reliance cap is ₹5 crore, your next query should look for the enterprise standard, not repeat the first. - Be specific. Vague queries waste a retrieval. - Set is_complete=true as soon as you can answer; do not over-gather.""" def iterative_retrieval(question, retrievers, max_steps=4, model="gpt-4o-mini"): """Sequential retrieval where each step is informed by the last.""" gathered, trace = [], [] for step in range(max_steps): summary = "\n\n".join( f"[Step {i+1}] Query: {g['query']}\nFound: {g['summary']}" for i, g in enumerate(gathered) ) or "(nothing retrieved yet)" completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=RetrievalPlan, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": ITERATIVE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n\nEvidence so far:\n{summary}"}], ) plan = completion.choices[0].message.parsed trace.append({"step": step, "reasoning": plan.reasoning, "complete": plan.is_complete}) if plan.is_complete or not plan.next_query: break docs = retrievers[plan.next_source](plan.next_query, k=5) gathered.append({ "query": plan.next_query, "source": plan.next_source, "docs": docs, "summary": _summarize_docs(docs, plan.next_query), }) all_docs = [d for g in gathered for d in g["docs"]] return {"documents": all_docs, "steps": len(gathered), "trace": trace} ``` **Summarising each step's results** rather than passing raw chunks keeps the planning context small. Passing five full chunks per step means step 4's planning prompt contains twenty chunks, which is expensive and dilutes the model's attention. **`is_complete` prevents over-gathering.** Without it the agent uses its full step budget on every query, including simple ones. ##### Adaptive retrieval decisions The cheapest and highest-return decision: whether to retrieve at all. ```python class RetrievalDecision(BaseModel): needs_retrieval: bool complexity: Literal["simple", "moderate", "complex"] estimated_retrievals: int = Field(..., ge=0, le=4) reasoning: str ADAPTIVE_SYSTEM = """Decide how much retrieval this question needs. needs_retrieval=false for: greetings, meta-questions, clarifications about your previous answer, general knowledge. complexity: - simple: one lookup (estimated_retrievals=1) - moderate: needs rewriting or two sources (2) - complex: comparison or multi-hop (3-4)""" def adaptive_rag(question, conversation, retrievers, generator): completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.0, response_format=RetrievalDecision, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": ADAPTIVE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}], ) decision = completion.choices[0].message.parsed if not decision.needs_retrieval: return {"answer": generator(question, conversation=conversation), "mode": "direct", "retrievals": 0} if decision.complexity == "simple": docs = retrievers["contracts"](question, k=5) graded = grade_documents(question, docs) if graded["n_relevant"]: return {"answer": rag_generate(question, graded["relevant"]), "mode": "single_shot", "retrievals": 1} # fall through to the agent loop result = iterative_retrieval(question, retrievers, max_steps=decision.estimated_retrievals) return {"answer": rag_generate(question, result["documents"][:8]), "mode": "iterative", "retrievals": result["steps"]} ``` **Route simple queries down the fast path.** On a realistic mixed workload, 60–70% of queries are simple and should never enter the agent loop. That routing is what keeps median latency acceptable while the tail handles the hard cases. ##### Measuring the trade ```python import time import numpy as np def compare_rag_modes(eval_set, static_fn, agentic_fn, price_per_1k_in=0.0125, price_per_1k_out=0.05): """Accuracy, latency, and cost for static versus agentic.""" rows = [] for name, fn in [("static", static_fn), ("agentic", agentic_fn)]: by_type = {} for item in eval_set: t0 = time.perf_counter() out = fn(item["question"]) latency = time.perf_counter() - t0 correct = _judge_correct(out["answer"], item["reference"]) tokens = out.get("tokens_in", 0), out.get("tokens_out", 0) cost = (tokens[0] / 1000 * price_per_1k_in + tokens[1] / 1000 * price_per_1k_out) qtype = item.get("query_type", "simple") by_type.setdefault(qtype, []).append((correct, latency, cost, out.get("retrievals", 1))) row = {"mode": name} for qtype, vals in by_type.items(): row[f"acc_{qtype}"] = round(float(np.mean([v[0] for v in vals])), 3) allv = [v for vals in by_type.values() for v in vals] row["p50_s"] = round(float(np.percentile([v[1] for v in allv], 50)), 2) row["p95_s"] = round(float(np.percentile([v[1] for v in allv], 95)), 2) row["inr_per_query"] = round(float(np.mean([v[2] for v in allv])), 4) row["mean_retrievals"] = round(float(np.mean([v[3] for v in allv])), 2) rows.append(row) return rows ``` A representative result: | Mode | acc_simple | acc_comparison | acc_multihop | p50 | p95 | ₹/query | retrievals | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | static | **0.91** | 0.34 | 0.28 | **1.4s** | **2.1s** | **0.012** | 1.00 | | agentic (always) | 0.89 | **0.86** | **0.81** | 4.9s | 11.2s | 0.058 | 2.7 | | **agentic (adaptive)** | 0.90 | 0.85 | 0.79 | **1.8s** | 8.4s | **0.024** | 1.6 | **Three findings worth internalising.** Agentic RAG is marginally *worse* on simple queries — the extra grading step occasionally discards a good document. It is dramatically better on comparison and multi-hop. And adaptive routing captures nearly all the benefit at a third of the median latency. ##### Common mistakes - **No iteration bounds**, allowing infinite retrieve-rewrite loops. - **Sequential document grading**, adding seconds of latency. - **Grading with a large model** when a small one or a cross-encoder suffices. - **Running the agent loop on every query** instead of routing simple ones to a fast path. - **Conflating ungrounded and incomplete answers** — they need different corrections. - **Passing raw chunks into planning prompts** instead of summaries. - **No trace**, making a multi-step system undebuggable. - **Parallel retrieval for genuinely sequential multi-hop questions.** - **Over-gathering** because the agent has no `is_complete` signal. - **Measuring aggregate accuracy** instead of breaking down by query type — the aggregate hides that agentic is worse on simple queries. - **Ignoring p95 latency.** An 11-second tail is unusable in chat even if the median is fine. ##### Hands-on: build the cycle Your practical task builds a LangGraph agent that retrieves, grades, and re-queries when documents are insufficient. Get the cycle working first with hard bounds, then verify it actually loops — feed it a query using terminology absent from your corpus and confirm the rewrite path fires. Print the trace for every query; the sequence of nodes visited is what makes the agent comprehensible. The mini project adds document grading, query rewriting, and web-search fallback. Instrument the fallback carefully: log how often it fires and whether the web results actually improved the answer. In many corpora the fallback fires on questions that genuinely have no answer, and refusing would be better than answering from the open web — that is a product decision worth surfacing. The assignment compares static and agentic RAG on hard queries, quantifying accuracy, latency, and cost. **Segment by query type.** The single most important number in your write-up is the accuracy gap on multi-hop questions against the latency cost on simple ones, because that ratio is what justifies or kills the architecture for a given product. ##### Key takeaways - **Agentic RAG's advantage is recognising its own failures at runtime** — grading retrieved documents and re-querying is what fixes the multi-hop and vocabulary-mismatch categories. - **Every cycle needs a hard bound.** `MAX_REWRITES` and `MAX_RETRIEVALS` are what separate an agent from an infinite loop. - **Grade documents in parallel with a small model** — sequential grading with a large model makes the architecture unusable in interactive products. - **Route simple queries to a fast path.** Adaptive retrieval captures most of the accuracy benefit at a fraction of the median latency. - **Ungrounded and incomplete are different failures**: regenerate for the first, retrieve more for the second, and measure your results broken down by query type.
practical_task_reference: Build a LangGraph agent that retrieves, grades relevance, and re-queries when documents are insufficient.
mini_project_reference: Create an agentic RAG assistant with document grading, query rewriting, and web-search fallback.
assignment_reference: Compare static RAG vs agentic RAG on hard queries and quantify accuracy, latency, and cost differences.
